newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Budget-Govt to target tax breaks.
newsitem.headline: Australia Budget-Govt to target tax breaks.

text.p: Australia's conservative government goes into its second deficit-cutting budget next week with its sights on tax concessions which cost A$17 billion a year and which could help finally eliminate Canberra's deficit.

Economists expect the government to announce a A$2 billion underlying deficit -- that is, excluding asset sales -- for the year to June 1998, although most of them base their estimates on government fiscal projections that now look pessimistic.
Treasurer Peter Costello will deliver his 1997/98 budget in parliament at 0930 GMT (7.30 p.m.) on Tuesday, May 13.

With the government expected to raise A$8 billion or more from selling a third of telecommunications carrier Telstra Corp, the overall or "headline" budget balance is expected to be a surplus of A$6 billion or more, the highest since 1990/91.

If the government implements the A$1.8 billion in cuts that the economists expect and the no-policy-change budget position is really better than forecast, as the latest fiscal data suggests, then Costello will pull a rabbit out of the hat next week and announce a budget close to balance.

Successive waves of cuts and a steadily expanding economy have brought down the underlying deficit to probably less than A$8.5 billion in the year to June 1997, compared with a post-recession peak of A$17.1 billion in 1993/94.

The government is committed to eliminating the budget deficit by 1998/99, but its latest projections, which some analysts call pessimistic, show the budget heading for a deficit of A$3.9 billion in 1997/98 and A$2.2 billion in 1998/99.

So, yet more savings will be announced next week and the government, caught between the difficulty of finding more spending cuts and its promise to not raise taxes, is expected to eliminate some of the exemptions that many taxpayers enjoy.

Costello flagged so-called taxation expenditures in last year's budget and in January's mid-year review he estimated that the concessions would cost the government A$16.7 billion in lost revenue in 1996/97, rising to A$18.9 billion in 1999/2000.

"The government intends to review all existing tax expenditures to ascertain the extent to which they are contributing towards the achievement of its policy goals, and whether some tax expenditures might be converted to outlays programmes to achieve a better outcome," last year's budget papers said.
Economists see little challenge in the government cutting the 1997/98 budget by A$2 billion, compared with the A$7 billion cuts for the same fiscal year projected in last year's budget.
Citibank economist Annette Beacher expects cuts in the order of A$2.5 billion.

Since she thinks the budget is in better condition than official projections show, this should produce an underlying balance near zero and maybe a headline surplus near A$10 billion -- the highest ever, disregarding inflation.
Beacher sees the risk to this forecast in the potential for new spending initiatives, especially in the labour market programmes that the government wound back last year.
"Unemployment is going to be around for a long time and we need a renewed commitment to education and training," she said.
The January budget estimates now look pessimistic because the latest monthly financial reports have shown fiscal progress is ahead of schedule.
Compared with the A$8.5 billion underlying deficit forecast for the year to June, the 12 months to March have already produced a deficit down to A$6.2 billion.
The deficit forecast will be bettered unless fiscal performance in the final three months of the year is substantially worse than the previous year.
